{{Source citation|date=January 2020|qq=}}
'''Rekichū Gedan''' (暦注下段) is the calendrical annotation originally written at the very bottom of the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} that gives the daily auspices (the omens of good and bad fortune). It is also simply called the '''lower section'''. It is based on the divination method of the agricultural calendar – the {{ill|Agricultural Calendar|ja|農暦|lt=Peasant’s Calendar|lt_ja=農民曆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Agricultural Calendar|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中国暦|1=Chinese calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134032}}, which has been handed down since ancient China – and many of its contents (such as Ten‐sha Days and Jushi Days) overlap with those of the peasant’s calendar.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=查詢農民曆─農民曆/農曆/黃曆｜科技紫微網 |url=https://ecal.click108.com.twindex.php/ |website=ecal.click108.com.twindex.php |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=2023農民曆吉時查詢,黃曆通書黃道吉日查詢 - 農民曆查詢 |url=http://www.nongli.info/huangli/ |website=www.nongli.info |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=子易預測網 - 擇日萬年曆 |url=https://forecasting.hk/calendar/ |website=forecasting.hk |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=農民曆專有名詞 @ Gloria隨筆 :: 痞客邦 :: |url=http://andafansia.pixnet.net/blog/post/40052541 |website=Gloria隨筆 |date=2011-12-11 |access-date=2023-07-20 |language=zh-TW |last=Andafansia (Andafansia)|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=你應該懂的農民曆常識！搞懂「當日紀要」神祉，挑對日子趨吉避凶不求人 {{!|qq=}} 食尚玩家 |url=https://supertaste.tvbs.com.tw/hot/321211 |website=TVBS |date=2020-02-06 |access-date=2023-07-20 |last=TVBS|qq=}}</ref>
== List == Originally, in the lower section of the calendrical annotations, the Jushi Day (marked with “●”) and the Jūshi Day (sometimes written as “十し”) were not recorded in duplication with other items, while the other annotations often appeared several times on a single day – and on occasion the lower section was left blank. However, nowadays, with the prominence of systems such as {{ill|Rokuyō|ja|六曜|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rokuyō|qq=}} and {{ill|Nine Stars|ja|九星|1=Nine Stars|2=ja|3=九星|lt=Nine Stars|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nine Stars|qq=}}, the lower section has become rather minor; as a result, contemporary commercially available calendars sometimes omit the lower section entirely, or—if they include it—only record one or two annotations per day, and even if multiple annotations are recorded, even the Jushi or Jūshi Days are often duplicated with others.
In the period from the Meiji era to prewar Shōwa, the lower section of calendrical annotations found in the so‐called {{ill|Obake Calendar|ja|お化け暦|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Obake Calendar|1=obake-goyomi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11262936}} was not supervised by calendrical experts and frequently did not conform at all to the original method of determining the lower section.
Because the lower section of calendrical annotations is relatively minor in modern Japan, it is seldom included in calendars that use the seven-day format.
=== Auspicious Days === The auspicious days in these lower calendrical annotations are known as the '''Seven Auspicious Days'''.
==== Ten‐sha Day ==== (Tensha nichi, tenshabi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as “天しや” and also appears in the {{ill|Day Selection|ja|選日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection|1=Senjitsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60988968}}. It is regarded as the day on which the myriad deities ascend to heaven and where heaven forgives the sins of all things – making it the most auspicious day of all. Accordingly, only on Ten‐sha Day is the annotation “万よし” (all is auspicious) added. Ten‐sha Days are determined by the season and the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac}} and occur five or six times a year. {| class="wikitable" |- | From the start of Spring to the day before the start of Summer || 戊寅日 |- | From the start of Summer to the day before the start of Autumn || 甲午日 |- | From the start of Autumn to the day before the start of Winter || 戊申日 |- | From the start of Winter to the day before the start of Spring || 甲子日 |}
==== Kamiyoshi Day ==== (Kamiyoshi nichi, kamiyoshi bi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as “神よし”. It is considered auspicious for matters related to divine rites – that is, for visiting shrines, participating in festivals, and honoring one’s ancestors – while it is inauspicious for impure matters. This calendrical annotation is unique to Japan. Kamiyoshi Days are determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}) and are allocated among the following 33 zodiac designations (the numbers indicate the number of days from the first Jiazi Day, 甲子日):
2乙丑日・4丁卯日・6己巳日・7庚午日・9壬申日・10癸酉日・14丁丑日・16己卯日・19壬午日・21甲申日・22乙酉日・25戊子日・28辛卯日・31甲午日・33丙申日・34丁酉日・36己亥日・37庚子日・38辛丑日・40癸卯日・42乙巳日・43丙午日・44丁未日・45戊申日・46己酉日・48辛亥日・49壬子日・52乙卯日・55戊午日・56己未日・57庚申日・58辛酉日
==== Daimyō Day ==== (Daimyō nichi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as “大みやう”. The term “Daimyō” signifies a day when heaven and earth are fully open and the sun shines in every corner, making it extremely auspicious for all benevolent activities. It is especially favorable for construction, relocation, and travel. Daimyō Day first appeared as a calendrical annotation in the Tang dynasty’s {{ill|Daimyō Calendar|ja|大明暦|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daimyō Calendar|1=Daimyō Calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5369150}}. It is determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}) and is allocated among the following 25 zodiac designations (the numbers indicate the count from the first Jiazi Day). (There is also a theory that, excluding the four designations 6己巳日, 7庚午日, 44丁未日, and 55戊午日, only 21 types apply.)
6己巳日・7庚午日・8辛未日・9壬申日・10癸酉日・14丁丑日・16己卯日・19壬午日・21甲申日・24丁亥日・29壬辰日・32乙未日・39壬寅日・41甲辰日・42乙巳日・43丙午日・44丁未日・46己酉日・47庚戌日・48辛亥日・53丙辰日・55戊午日・56己未日・57庚申日・58辛酉日
==== Kishuku Day ==== (Kishuku nichi) is determined in the same manner as the auspices of the {{ill|Twenty-Eight Mansions|en|Twenty-Eight Mansions|WD=Q1378760|lt=Twenty‐Eight Mansions}}’ “{{ill|Ghost (Chinese constellation)|en|Ghost (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145465|lt=Kishuku}}.”
==== Tenon Day ==== (Tenon nichi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as “天おん”. As its name implies, it is a day on which one receives the blessings of heaven, and is used for auspicious matters – though it must not be used for inauspicious affairs. Tenon Day is determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}). Although various theories exist regarding its allocation, the ''Rekirin Mondōshu'' designates the following 15 zodiac days (the numbers indicate the count from the first Jiazi Day):
1甲子日・2乙丑日・3丙寅日・4丁卯日・5戊辰日・16己卯日・17庚辰日・18辛巳日・19壬午日・20癸未日・46己酉日・47庚戌日・48辛亥日・49壬子日・50癸丑日
==== Bosō Day ==== (Bosō nichi) is simply written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as '''母倉'''. It signifies a day when heaven shows benevolence toward humankind in the same way a mother cares for her child, and is one of the '''Seven Auspicious Days'''. Everything is considered auspicious on this day – and marriage in particular is viewed as extremely favorable. Likewise, construction and renovation are also auspicious. Bosō Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated to the following day.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month and Pig Month || Monkey Day and Rooster Day |- | Ox Month, Dragon Month, Goat Month, and Dog Month || Snake Day and Horse Day |- | Tiger Month and Rabbit Month || Rat Day and Pig Day |- | Snake Month and Horse Month || Tiger Day and Rabbit Day |- | Monkey Month and Rooster Month || Ox Day, Dragon Day, Goat Day, and Dog Day |}
==== Tsukitoku Day ==== (Tsukitoku nichi, gattoku nichi) is considered auspicious for activities involving the soil, such as the expansion or renovation of a house. Tsukitoku Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated to the following day.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month, Dragon Month, and Monkey Month || 壬日 |- | Ox Month, Snake Month, and Rooster Month || 庚日 |- | Tiger Month, Horse Month, and Dog Month || 丙日 |- | Rabbit Month, Goat Month, and Pig Month || 甲日 |}
=== Inauspicious Days ===
==== Jushi Day ==== (Jushi nichi, jushibi), also known as the “Black Day” because it is marked with a “●” in the lower section of the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} (and sometimes written simply as “● Day” in modern calendars), is considered the worst of all inauspicious days. It is said that on this day one should not consult any other calendrical annotations, and that if one falls ill on this day, death is inevitable. Illness visits, taking medication, acupuncture, and travel are especially considered unlucky, though holding a funeral is permitted. Jushi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} as follows.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Rabbit Day |- | Ox Month || Rooster Day |- | Tiger Month || Dog Day |- | Rabbit Month || Dragon Day |- | Dragon Month || Pig Day |- | Snake Month || Snake Day |- | Horse Month || Rat Day |- | Goat Month || Horse Day |- | Monkey Month || Ox Day |- | Rooster Month || Goat Day |- | Dog Month || Tiger Day |- | Pig Month || Monkey Day |}
==== Jūshi Day ==== (Jūshi nichi) is sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as “十し”. It is regarded as inauspicious in every respect – coming immediately after Jushi Day (the Black Day) – and is considered unfavorable for all matters, although unlike Jushi Day, holding a funeral is not strictly prohibited. Jūshi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and follows a repeating cycle of Rooster, Snake, and Ox. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Snake Day |- | Ox Month || Ox Day |- | Tiger Month || Rooster Day |- | Rabbit Month || Snake Day |- | Dragon Month || Ox Day |- | Snake Month || Rooster Day |- | Horse Month || Snake Day |- | Goat Month || Ox Day |- | Monkey Month || Rooster Day |- | Rooster Month || Snake Day |- | Dog Month || Ox Day |- | Pig Month || Rooster Day |}
==== Five Tomb Days ==== (Five Tomb Days) vary from person to person according to the nature of the {{ill|Noin|ja|納音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Noin|1=natchin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10465180}} of one’s birth year, and are determined as shown in the table below. The term “Five Tombs” refers to the fact that the zodiac signs of {{ill|Ox|ja|丑|1=chǒu (丑)|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16539206}}, {{ill|Dragon|ja|辰|1=chén|lt=Dragon (辰)|2=ja|3=辰|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dragon|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16538966}}, {{ill|Goat|ja|未|1=wèi|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q20128396}}, and {{ill|Dog (zodiac)|en|Dog (zodiac)|WD=Q755126|lt=Dog (戌)}} – which possess an earth element – designate these five types of zodiac days as Five Tomb Days. All Five Tomb Days are inauspicious; while they pose no problem for building a house, activities such as groundbreaking, foundation laying, funerals, tomb construction, sowing ({{ill|Sowing|en|Sowing|WD=Q777671|lt=Sowing}}), travel, and prayer are considered unlucky. By its very name, it is said that carrying out such activities (especially funerals) on these days will result in “five tombs” (i.e. the death of five people). {| class="wikitable" |- | (Wood element) || 乙丑日 |- | (Fire element) || 丙戌日 |- | (Earth element) || 戊辰日 |- | (Metal element) || 辛未日 |- | (Water element) || 壬辰日 |}
==== Kiki Day ==== (Kiki nichi, also read as kishibi, kikojitsu, or kiimi nichi) is sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} simply as “きこ”. In modern calendars, even lending or borrowing money is considered inauspicious on this day. Kiki Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}, and is allocated as follows.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat, Rabbit, Horse, and Rooster Months || Tiger Day |- | Ox, Dragon, Goat, and Dog Months || Rat Day |- | Tiger, Snake, Monkey, and Pig Months || Ox Day |}
==== Chikibi Day ==== (Chikibi nichi, also read as chii nichi or chikoni nichi) is sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as “ちいみ”. It refers to the influence of the spirit of the ρ, σ, and ε stars of the {{ill|Boötes|en|Boötes|WD=Q8667|lt=Ushikai}}—which in China are known as “Sakki”, “Nichiki”, and “Chikiki” and are believed to govern a murderous energy. On Chikibi Day, the sight of blood is considered particularly inauspicious, and activities such as acupuncture, capital punishment, and hunting are especially taboo. An ancient calendrical annotation, it is noted in the detailed calendars that “one must not use needles to draw blood on this day.” Chikibi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Horse Day |- | Ox Month || Rat Day |- | Tiger Month || Ox Day |- | Rabbit Month || Goat Day |- | Dragon Month || Tiger Day |- | Snake Month || Monkey Day |- | Horse Month || Rabbit Day |- | Goat Month || Rooster Day |- | Monkey Month || Dragon Day |- | Rooster Month || Dog Day |- | Dog Month || Snake Day |- | Pig Month || Pig Day |}
==== Tenka Day ==== (Tenka nichi, tenka bi), corresponding to {{ill|Chika Day|ja|地火日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chika Day|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 暦注下段|1=rekichuugedan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514957}}, is also known as one of the “Five Poor Days.” According to the Five Elements theory, fire is divided into three types—heavenly fire, earthly fire, and human fire—with Tenka referring to the severe fire of heaven. It is said that if one undertakes activities such as raising a roof or re-roofing on a Tenka Day, a fire is inevitable. Likewise, repairs to a house or relocation (in the sense of a distinguished person moving) are considered inauspicious. Tenka Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows. (Its allocation is exactly the same as that for Wōryaku Day, one of the Three Bad Days.) Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat, Dragon, and Monkey Months || Horse Day |- | Ox, Snake, and Rooster Months || Rooster Day |- | Tiger, Horse, and Dog Months || Rat Day |- | Rabbit, Goat, and Pig Months || Rabbit Day |}
==== Chika Day (“Shishin” in the Agricultural Calendar) ==== (Chika nichi, chika bi) corresponds to Tenka Day. In the Chinese {{ill|Agricultural Calendar|ja|農暦|lt=Peasant’s Calendar|lt_ja=農民曆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Agricultural Calendar|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中国暦|1=Chinese calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134032}}, it is called “'''Shishin'''” (the God of Death) and is treated as equivalent to Jushi Day. According to the Five Elements theory, fire is divided into heavenly, earthly, and human fire, with “earthly fire” referring to the severe fire of the earth. On Chika Day, activities such as groundbreaking, laying foundations, erecting pillars, well digging, sowing ({{ill|Sowing|en|Sowing|WD=Q777671|lt=Sowing}}), tomb construction, and funerals are considered inauspicious. Chika Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows. This allocation is exactly the same as that for “Hira” in the Twelve Directives, although what is deemed inauspicious on Chika Day is considered auspicious under “Hira,” resulting in a contradiction. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Rabbit Day |- | Ox Month || Dragon Day |- | Tiger Month || Snake Day |- | Rabbit Month || Horse Day |- | Dragon Month || Goat Day |- | Snake Month || Monkey Day |- | Horse Month || Rooster Day |- | Goat Month || Dog Day |- | Monkey Month || Pig Day |- | Rooster Month || Rat Day |- | Dog Month || Ox Day |- | Pig Month || Tiger Day |}
==== Kyōkai Day ==== (Kyōkai nichi, kyōkebi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as “くゑ日” (sometimes rendered as “くしえ” or “くしゑ”). It is a day on which the harmony of yin and yang fails, making it a taboo day for all matters; any auspicious undertaking on this day is considered inauspicious. This is one of the older calendrical annotations – in the detailed annotated calendars it is recorded under 24 different names (as indicated in square brackets in the table below). In the Senmei Calendar it appears 82 times per year, and was reduced to 72 times in the Teikyou Calendar. Although various theories exist regarding its allocation, during the Senmei Calendar era it was determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}, whereas from the Teikyou Calendar onward it was determined by the monthly method (based on the {{ill|Old Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}}). Kyōkai Day is fixed for each month by assigning a specific {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac}}; in the table below the items in parentheses were abolished in the Teikyou Calendar (with <sup>●</sup> indicating those overlapping with Jushi Day and <sup>十</sup> those overlapping with Jūshi Day). Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- ! Birth Month !! Designated Days |- | Rat Month || 戊子日 [陰陽倶錯] ・ 丙午日 [陰陽衝撃] ・ 壬子日 [陰陽倶錯] |- | Ox Month || 戊子日 [遂陣] ・ 丁未日 [陰陽倶錯] ・ 壬子日 [遂陣] ・ (癸丑日 [陽錯] <sup>十</sup>) ・ 癸亥日 [陰錯] |- | Tiger Month || 辛卯日 [三陰] ・ (庚戌日 [陰錯] <sup>●</sup>) ・ 甲寅日 [陽錯] |- | Rabbit Month || 己卯日 [陰道衝陽] ・ 乙卯日 [陽錯] ・ 辛酉日 [陽錯] |- | Dragon Month || 甲子日 [絶陰] ・ 乙丑日 [絶陰] ・ 丙寅日 [絶陰] ・ 丁卯日 [絶陰] ・ 戊辰日 [単陰] ・ 壬申日 [孤辰] ・ 戊申日 [孤辰] ・ 庚辰日 [陰位] ・ 甲申日 [行很] ・ 甲辰日 [陽錯] ・ 丙申日 [了戻] ・ 甲辰日 [陽錯] ・ 庚申日 [陰錯孤辰] ・ (癸亥日 [絶陰] <sup>●</sup>) |- | Snake Month || 戊辰日 [絶陰] ・ (己巳日 [陽錯絶陽] <sup>●</sup>) ・ 辛未日 [孤辰] ・ 癸未日 [孤辰] ・ 乙未日 [行很] ・ 己亥日 [陰陽衝破] ・ 丙午日 [歳博] ・ 丁未日 [陰錯了戻] ・ (丁巳日 [陽錯] <sup>●</sup>) ・ 戊午日 [歳博] ・ 己未日 [陰錯孤辰] ・ 癸亥日 [陰陽交破] |- | Horse Month || 丙午日 [陰陽倶錯] ・ (壬子日 [陰陽衝撃] <sup>●</sup>) ・ 戊午日 [陰陽倶錯] |- | Goat Month || 己巳日 [陰錯] ・ 丙午日 [遂陣] ・ 丁未日 [陽錯] ・ (癸丑日 [陽破陰衝] <sup>十</sup>) ・ 丁巳日 [陰錯] ・ (戊午日 [遂陣] <sup>●</sup>) ・ 己未日 [陽錯] |- | Monkey Month || 乙酉日 [三陰] ・ 甲辰日 [陰錯] ・ 庚申日 [陽錯] |- | Rooster Month || 己酉日 [陰道衝陽] ・ 乙卯日 [陰錯] ・ 辛酉日 [陽錯] |- | Dog Month || (丙寅日 [孤辰] <sup>●</sup>) ・ 甲戌日 [陰位] ・ (戊寅日 [孤辰] <sup>●</sup>) ・ (庚寅日 [行很] <sup>●</sup>) ・ 辛卯日 [絶陽] ・ 壬辰日 [絶陽] ・ 癸巳日 [絶陽] ・ 甲午日 [絶陽] ・ 乙未日 [絶陽] ・ 丙申日 [絶陽] ・ 丁酉日 [絶陽] ・ 戊戌日 [単陽] ・ (壬寅日 [了戻] <sup>●</sup>) ・ 庚戌日 [陽錯] ・ 甲寅日 [陰錯孤辰] <sup>●</sup> |- | Pig Month || 乙丑日 [孤辰] ・ 己巳日 [陰陽衝破] ・ 丁丑日 [孤辰] ・ 戊子日 [歳博] ・ 己丑日 [孤辰] ・ 戊戌日 [絶陽] ・ 己亥日 [絶陰] ・ 辛丑日 [行很] ・ 壬子日 [歳博] ・ 癸丑日 [陰錯了戻] ・ 丁巳日 [陰陽交破] ・ 癸亥日 [陽錯] |}
Incidentally, in the detailed annotated calendars, on days that are not designated as Kyōkai Days, inscriptions for the Great Age God and the Small Age God – such as “After the Great Age”, “Great/Small Age Position”, or “Before the Great Age, in contrast to the Small Age” – were written; on Kyōkai Days, however, the name corresponding to one of the 24 types of Kyōkai Days was inscribed instead. In kana calendars, the detailed classification of Kyōkai Days was omitted, and only the notation “くゑ日” appears in the lower section.
==== Ōmō Day ==== (Ōmō nichi) literally means “the day to depart and perish.” In ancient times, military campaigns or long journeys were taboo on this day, and official audiences, relocations, or weddings were also considered inauspicious. Ōmō Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} based on the number of days from each month’s seasonal marker. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || 20th day |- | Ox Month || 30th day |- | Tiger Month || 7th day |- | Rabbit Month || 14th day |- | Dragon Month || 21st day |- | Snake Month || 8th day |- | Horse Month || 16th day |- | Goat Month || 24th day |- | Monkey Month || 9th day |- | Rooster Month || 18th day |- | Dog Month || 27th day |- | Pig Month || 10th day |}
==== The Three Bad Days ==== The term “Three Bad Days” (sanga no akunichi) is the collective name for the three inauspicious days: Daimaka Day, Wōryaku Day, and Mettomon Day. Their allocation varies according to the individual’s birth year’s {{ill|Earthly Branches|en|Earthly Branches|WD=Q1072961|lt=Chinese Zodiac}}. For example, for someone born in the Year of the Snake, the fourth month (the taboo month) will have its Monkey Day, Rooster Day, and Tiger Day designated as the Three Bad Days; likewise, in January only those born in the Year of the Tiger and in February only those born in the Year of the Rabbit are affected. However, some modern calendars list all the days indicated in the table below as inauspicious for everyone, regardless of one’s birth year. The Three Bad Days should not be used for any auspicious undertaking, and are considered extremely inauspicious for Buddhist ceremonies. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" ! Birth Year !! Taboo Month !! Daimaka Day !! Wōryaku Day !! Mettomon Day |- | Rat Year || Rat Month || Rooster Day || Horse Day || Rabbit Day |- | Ox Year || Ox Month || Dragon Day || Rooster Day || Dog Day |- | Tiger Year || Tiger Month || Pig Day || Rat Day || Snake Day |- | Rabbit Year || Rabbit Month || Horse Day || Rabbit Day || Rat Day |- | Dragon Year || Dragon Month || Ox Day || Horse Day || Goat Day |- | Snake Year || Snake Month || Monkey Day || Rooster Day || Tiger Day |- | Horse Year || Horse Month || Rabbit Day || Rat Day || Rooster Day |- | Goat Year || Goat Month || Dog Day || Rabbit Day || Dragon Day |- | Monkey Year || Monkey Month || Snake Day || Horse Day || Pig Day |- | Rooster Year || Rooster Month || Rat Day || Rooster Day || Horse Day |- | Dog Year || Dog Month || Goat Day || Rat Day || Ox Day |- | Pig Year || Pig Month || Tiger Day || Rabbit Day || Monkey Day |}
===== Daimaka Day ===== (Daimaka nichi) is considered the worst of the Three Bad Days. It is advised to refrain from excessive talk, and to strictly avoid home repairs, construction of doorways, sea voyages, and funerals.
===== Wōryaku Day ===== (Rōshaku nichi) is deemed inauspicious for all undertakings. It is said that engaging in any activity on this day will result in complete failure.
===== Mettomon Day ===== (Metsumon nichi) is regarded as inauspicious in every respect – it is said that acting on this day will, as the name implies, bring ruin to one’s entire family. There is also a day known in the calendrical annotations as “Metsubi” which is considered inauspicious for all matters; however, this arises from a mathematical discrepancy between the ideal 360-day year and the actual year, and is of an entirely different character. Moreover, the term “Metsubi” was abolished during the Teikyou Calendar reform in the Edo period and is no longer reflected in current lunar calendars. (Sometimes, Mettomon Day is abbreviated as “Metsubi,” leading to confusion between the two.)
==== Tokigejiki (Time‐Limited Eating Taboo) ==== (Tokigejiki, also known as Gejikodoki) is a designation for a specific time on a specific day that is considered inauspicious for eating. Like Saigejiki, it refers to the time when the spirit of the '''Tengūsei''' (Tengu Star) – a type of meteor – descends to the earthly realm for the purpose of eating. It is said that if a person eats during this time, all the nutritional value of the food will be absorbed by the spirit, and consuming any leftovers will bring misfortune. In addition to meals, activities such as sowing seeds, opening a rice bag, bathing, and planting are also considered inauspicious during this period. The day and time for Tokigejiki are as follows. The month is determined by the seasonal transition; for example, in January, the Hai period of Goat Day is designated as Tokigejiki. (In calendars from the Teikyou era onward, only the months of May through October are indicated.) Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Ox Day during the Rooster Hour |- | Ox Month || Rabbit Day during the Dog Hour |- | Tiger Month || Goat Day during the Pig Hour |- | Rabbit Month || Dog Day during the Rat Hour |- | Dragon Month || Dragon Day during the Ox Hour |- | Snake Month || Tiger Day during the Tiger Hour |- | Horse Month || Horse Day during the Rabbit Hour |- | Goat Month || Rat Day during the Dragon Hour |- | Monkey Month || Monkey Day during the Snake Hour |- | Rooster Month || Rooster Day during the Horse Hour |- | Dog Month || Snake Day during the Goat Hour |- | Pig Month || Pig Day during the Monkey Hour |}
==== Saigejiki (Year‐Long Eating Taboo) ==== (Saigejiki, also read as Saikajiki) is, like Tokigejiki, the designation for the day on which the spirit of the '''Tengūsei''' (Tengu Star) descends to the earthly realm for the purpose of eating; however, unlike Tokigejiki, Saigejiki is not tied to a specific time. It is considered a mildly inauspicious day, and if another auspicious annotation is present on the same day, there is no need to avoid it; however, if it coincides with other inauspicious days, its effects are compounded. This day is also regarded as a day to refrain from heavy meals and excessive drinking, and, like Tokigejiki, activities such as sowing seeds or opening rice bags and planting are considered inauspicious. Saigejiki is allocated to a specific {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac}} day that varies according to the individual’s birth year ({{ill|Earthly Branches|en|Earthly Branches|WD=Q1072961|lt=Chinese Zodiac}}). The numbers indicate the count from the first Jiazi Day. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Year || 14 || 丁丑日 |- | Ox Year || 27 || 庚寅日 |- | Tiger Year || 4 || 丁卯日 |- | Rabbit Year || 29 || 壬辰日 |- | Dragon Year || 54 || 丁巳日 |- | Snake Year || 43 || 丙午日 |- | Horse Year || 44 || 丁未日 |- | Goat Year || 57 || 庚申日 |- | Monkey Year || 34 || 丁酉日 |- | Rooster Year || 23 || 丙戌日 |- | Dog Year || 48 || 辛亥日 |- | Pig Year || 5 || 庚子日 |}
=== Others ===
==== Juuni Day ==== (Juuni nichi, sometimes written as “Chiu nichi”) is designated on days when the yang (陽) aspect is compounded on Snake Days (巳) and when the yin (陰) is compounded on Pig Days (亥). It is believed that actions performed on this day will have a compounded effect – making auspicious matters even more so and inauspicious matters even worse. However, marriages are considered unfavorable on this day as they may lead to remarriage. Additionally, any day on which the numeral of the month and the day coincide is also referred to as Juuni Day.
==== Fuku Day ==== (Fuku nichi or buku nichi), sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar}} as “ぶく日”, is a day on which the effects of any action are said to be doubled – if an auspicious act is undertaken, the auspiciousness is compounded, and if an inauspicious act is undertaken, the misfortune is compounded. However, weddings are considered inauspicious on this day as they may lead to remarriage. Fuku Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month and Horse Month || 丁日 and 癸日 |- | Ox Month, Dragon Month, Goat Month, and Dog Month || 戊日 and 己日 |- | Tiger Month and Monkey Month || 甲日 and 庚日 |- | Rabbit Month and Rooster Month || 乙日 and 辛日 |- | Snake Month and Pig Month || 丙日 and 壬日 |}

{{Source citation|date=January 2020|qq=}}
'''Rekichū Gedan''' (暦注下段) is the calendrical annotation originally written at the very bottom of the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} that gives the daily auspices (the omens of good and bad fortune). It is also simply called the '''lower section'''. It is based on the divination method of the agricultural calendar – the {{ill|Agricultural Calendar|ja|農暦|lt=Peasant’s Calendar|lt_ja=農民曆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Agricultural Calendar|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中国暦|1=Chinese calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134032}}, which has been handed down since ancient China – and many of its contents (such as Ten‐sha Days and Jushi Days) overlap with those of the peasant’s calendar.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=查詢農民曆─農民曆/農曆/黃曆｜科技紫微網 |url=https://ecal.click108.com.twindex.php/ |website=ecal.click108.com.twindex.php |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=2023農民曆吉時查詢,黃曆通書黃道吉日查詢 - 農民曆查詢 |url=http://www.nongli.info/huangli/ |website=www.nongli.info |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=子易預測網 - 擇日萬年曆 |url=https://forecasting.hk/calendar/ |website=forecasting.hk |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=農民曆專有名詞 @ Gloria隨筆 :: 痞客邦 :: |url=http://andafansia.pixnet.net/blog/post/40052541 |website=Gloria隨筆 |date=2011-12-11 |access-date=2023-07-20 |language=zh-TW |last=Andafansia (Andafansia)|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=你應該懂的農民曆常識！搞懂「當日紀要」神祉，挑對日子趨吉避凶不求人 {{!|qq=}} 食尚玩家 |url=https://supertaste.tvbs.com.tw/hot/321211 |website=TVBS |date=2020-02-06 |access-date=2023-07-20 |last=TVBS|qq=}}</ref>
== List == Originally, in the lower section of the calendrical annotations, the Jushi Day (marked with “●”) and the Jūshi Day (sometimes written as “十し”) were not recorded in duplication with other items, while the other annotations often appeared several times on a single day – and on occasion the lower section was left blank. However, nowadays, with the prominence of systems such as {{ill|Rokuyō|ja|六曜|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rokuyō|qq=}} and {{ill|Nine Stars|ja|九星|1=Nine Stars|2=ja|3=九星|lt=Nine Stars|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nine Stars|qq=}}, the lower section has become rather minor; as a result, contemporary commercially available calendars sometimes omit the lower section entirely, or—if they include it—only record one or two annotations per day, and even if multiple annotations are recorded, even the Jushi or Jūshi Days are often duplicated with others.
In the period from the Meiji era to prewar Shōwa, the lower section of calendrical annotations found in the so‐called {{ill|Obake Calendar|ja|お化け暦|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Obake Calendar|1=Ghost calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11262936}} was not supervised by calendrical experts and frequently did not conform at all to the original method of determining the lower section.
Because the lower section of calendrical annotations is relatively minor in modern Japan, it is seldom included in calendars that use the seven-day format.
=== Auspicious Days === The auspicious days in these lower calendrical annotations are known as the '''Seven Auspicious Days'''.
==== Ten‐sha Day ==== (Tensha nichi, tenshabi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “天しや” and also appears in the {{ill|Day Selection|ja|選日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection|1=Senjitsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60988968}}. It is regarded as the day on which the myriad deities ascend to heaven and where heaven forgives the sins of all things – making it the most auspicious day of all. Accordingly, only on Ten‐sha Day is the annotation “万よし” (all is auspicious) added. Ten‐sha Days are determined by the season and the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} and occur five or six times a year. {| class="wikitable" |- | From the start of Spring to the day before the start of Summer || 戊寅日 |- | From the start of Summer to the day before the start of Autumn || 甲午日 |- | From the start of Autumn to the day before the start of Winter || 戊申日 |- | From the start of Winter to the day before the start of Spring || 甲子日 |}
==== Kamiyoshi Day ==== (Kamiyoshi nichi, kamiyoshi bi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “神よし”. It is considered auspicious for matters related to divine rites – that is, for visiting shrines, participating in festivals, and honoring one’s ancestors – while it is inauspicious for impure matters. This calendrical annotation is unique to Japan. Kamiyoshi Days are determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}) and are allocated among the following 33 zodiac designations (the numbers indicate the number of days from the first Jiazi Day, 甲子日):
2乙丑日・4丁卯日・6己巳日・7庚午日・9壬申日・10癸酉日・14丁丑日・16己卯日・19壬午日・21甲申日・22乙酉日・25戊子日・28辛卯日・31甲午日・33丙申日・34丁酉日・36己亥日・37庚子日・38辛丑日・40癸卯日・42乙巳日・43丙午日・44丁未日・45戊申日・46己酉日・48辛亥日・49壬子日・52乙卯日・55戊午日・56己未日・57庚申日・58辛酉日
==== Daimyō Day ==== (Daimyō nichi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “大みやう”. The term “Daimyō” signifies a day when heaven and earth are fully open and the sun shines in every corner, making it extremely auspicious for all benevolent activities. It is especially favorable for construction, relocation, and travel. Daimyō Day first appeared as a calendrical annotation in the Tang dynasty’s {{ill|Daimyō Calendar|ja|大明暦|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daimyō Calendar|1=Q5369150|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5369150}}. It is determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}) and is allocated among the following 25 zodiac designations (the numbers indicate the count from the first Jiazi Day). (There is also a theory that, excluding the four designations 6己巳日, 7庚午日, 44丁未日, and 55戊午日, only 21 types apply.)
6己巳日・7庚午日・8辛未日・9壬申日・10癸酉日・14丁丑日・16己卯日・19壬午日・21甲申日・24丁亥日・29壬辰日・32乙未日・39壬寅日・41甲辰日・42乙巳日・43丙午日・44丁未日・46己酉日・47庚戌日・48辛亥日・53丙辰日・55戊午日・56己未日・57庚申日・58辛酉日
==== Kishuku Day ==== (Kishuku nichi) is determined in the same manner as the auspices of the {{ill|Twenty-Eight Mansions|en|Twenty-Eight Mansions|WD=Q1378760|lt=Twenty‐Eight Mansions|1=Twenty-Eight Mansions}}’ “{{ill|Ghost (Chinese constellation)|en|Ghost (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145465|lt=Kishuku|1=Ghost (Chinese constellation)}}.”
==== Tenon Day ==== (Tenon nichi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “天おん”. As its name implies, it is a day on which one receives the blessings of heaven, and is used for auspicious matters – though it must not be used for inauspicious affairs. Tenon Day is determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}). Although various theories exist regarding its allocation, the ''Rekirin Mondōshu'' designates the following 15 zodiac days (the numbers indicate the count from the first Jiazi Day):
1甲子日・2乙丑日・3丙寅日・4丁卯日・5戊辰日・16己卯日・17庚辰日・18辛巳日・19壬午日・20癸未日・46己酉日・47庚戌日・48辛亥日・49壬子日・50癸丑日
==== Bosō Day ==== (Bosō nichi) is simply written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as '''母倉'''. It signifies a day when heaven shows benevolence toward humankind in the same way a mother cares for her child, and is one of the '''Seven Auspicious Days'''. Everything is considered auspicious on this day – and marriage in particular is viewed as extremely favorable. Likewise, construction and renovation are also auspicious. Bosō Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated to the following day.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month and Pig Month || Monkey Day and Rooster Day |- | Ox Month, Dragon Month, Goat Month, and Dog Month || Snake Day and Horse Day |- | Tiger Month and Rabbit Month || Rat Day and Pig Day |- | Snake Month and Horse Month || Tiger Day and Rabbit Day |- | Monkey Month and Rooster Month || Ox Day, Dragon Day, Goat Day, and Dog Day |}
==== Tsukitoku Day ==== (Tsukitoku nichi, gattoku nichi) is considered auspicious for activities involving the soil, such as the expansion or renovation of a house. Tsukitoku Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated to the following day.

=== Inauspicious Days ===
==== Jushi Day ==== (Jushi nichi, jushibi), also known as the “Black Day” because it is marked with a “●” in the lower section of the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} (and sometimes written simply as “● Day” in modern calendars), is considered the worst of all inauspicious days. It is said that on this day one should not consult any other calendrical annotations, and that if one falls ill on this day, death is inevitable. Illness visits, taking medication, acupuncture, and travel are especially considered unlucky, though holding a funeral is permitted. Jushi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} as follows.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Rabbit Day |- | Ox Month || Rooster Day |- | Tiger Month || Dog Day |- | Rabbit Month || Dragon Day |- | Dragon Month || Pig Day |- | Snake Month || Snake Day |- | Horse Month || Rat Day |- | Goat Month || Horse Day |- | Monkey Month || Ox Day |- | Rooster Month || Goat Day |- | Dog Month || Tiger Day |- | Pig Month || Monkey Day |}
==== Jūshi Day ==== (Jūshi nichi) is sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “十し”. It is regarded as inauspicious in every respect – coming immediately after Jushi Day (the Black Day) – and is considered unfavorable for all matters, although unlike Jushi Day, holding a funeral is not strictly prohibited. Jūshi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and follows a repeating cycle of Rooster, Snake, and Ox. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Snake Day |- | Ox Month || Ox Day |- | Tiger Month || Rooster Day |- | Rabbit Month || Snake Day |- | Dragon Month || Ox Day |- | Snake Month || Rooster Day |- | Horse Month || Snake Day |- | Goat Month || Ox Day |- | Monkey Month || Rooster Day |- | Rooster Month || Snake Day |- | Dog Month || Ox Day |- | Pig Month || Rooster Day |}
==== Five Tomb Days ==== (Five Tomb Days) vary from person to person according to the nature of the {{ill|Noin|ja|納音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Noin|1=natchin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10465180}} of one’s birth year, and are determined as shown in the table below. The term “Five Tombs” refers to the fact that the zodiac signs of {{ill|Ox|ja|丑|1=chǒu|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16539206}}, {{ill|Dragon|ja|辰|1=chén|lt=Dragon (辰)|2=ja|3=辰|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dragon|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16538966}}, {{ill|Goat|ja|未|1=wèi|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q20128396}}, and {{ill|Dog (zodiac)|en|Dog (zodiac)|WD=Q755126|lt=Dog (戌)|1=Dog (zodiac)}} – which possess an earth element – designate these five types of zodiac days as Five Tomb Days. All Five Tomb Days are inauspicious; while they pose no problem for building a house, activities such as groundbreaking, foundation laying, funerals, tomb construction, sowing ({{ill|Sowing|en|Sowing|WD=Q777671|lt=Sowing|1=Sowing}}), travel, and prayer are considered unlucky. By its very name, it is said that carrying out such activities (especially funerals) on these days will result in “five tombs” (i.e. the death of five people). {| class="wikitable" |- | (Wood element) || 乙丑日 |- | (Fire element) || 丙戌日 |- | (Earth element) || 戊辰日 |- | (Metal element) || 辛未日 |- | (Water element) || 壬辰日 |}

==== Chikibi Day ==== (Chikibi nichi, also read as chii nichi or chikoni nichi) is sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “ちいみ”. It refers to the influence of the spirit of the ρ, σ, and ε stars of the {{ill|Boötes|en|Boötes|WD=Q8667|lt=Ushikai|1=Boötes}}—which in China are known as “Sakki”, “Nichiki”, and “Chikiki” and are believed to govern a murderous energy. On Chikibi Day, the sight of blood is considered particularly inauspicious, and activities such as acupuncture, capital punishment, and hunting are especially taboo. An ancient calendrical annotation, it is noted in the detailed calendars that “one must not use needles to draw blood on this day.” Chikibi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows.

==== Tenka Day ==== (Tenka nichi, tenka bi), corresponding to {{ill|Chika Day|ja|地火日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chika Day|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 暦注下段|1=Rekichū Gedan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514957}}, is also known as one of the “Five Poor Days.” According to the Five Elements theory, fire is divided into three types—heavenly fire, earthly fire, and human fire—with Tenka referring to the severe fire of heaven. It is said that if one undertakes activities such as raising a roof or re-roofing on a Tenka Day, a fire is inevitable. Likewise, repairs to a house or relocation (in the sense of a distinguished person moving) are considered inauspicious. Tenka Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows. (Its allocation is exactly the same as that for Wōryaku Day, one of the Three Bad Days.) Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat, Dragon, and Monkey Months || Horse Day |- | Ox, Snake, and Rooster Months || Rooster Day |- | Tiger, Horse, and Dog Months || Rat Day |- | Rabbit, Goat, and Pig Months || Rabbit Day |}
==== Chika Day (“Shishin” in the Agricultural Calendar) ==== (Chika nichi, chika bi) corresponds to Tenka Day. In the Chinese {{ill|Agricultural Calendar|ja|農暦|lt=Peasant’s Calendar|lt_ja=農民曆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Agricultural Calendar|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中国暦|1=Chinese calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134032}}, it is called “'''Shishin'''” (the God of Death) and is treated as equivalent to Jushi Day. According to the Five Elements theory, fire is divided into heavenly, earthly, and human fire, with “earthly fire” referring to the severe fire of the earth. On Chika Day, activities such as groundbreaking, laying foundations, erecting pillars, well digging, sowing ({{ill|Sowing|en|Sowing|WD=Q777671|lt=Sowing|1=Sowing}}), tomb construction, and funerals are considered inauspicious. Chika Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows. This allocation is exactly the same as that for “Hira” in the Twelve Directives, although what is deemed inauspicious on Chika Day is considered auspicious under “Hira,” resulting in a contradiction. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Rabbit Day |- | Ox Month || Dragon Day |- | Tiger Month || Snake Day |- | Rabbit Month || Horse Day |- | Dragon Month || Goat Day |- | Snake Month || Monkey Day |- | Horse Month || Rooster Day |- | Goat Month || Dog Day |- | Monkey Month || Pig Day |- | Rooster Month || Rat Day |- | Dog Month || Ox Day |- | Pig Month || Tiger Day |}
==== Kyōkai Day ==== (Kyōkai nichi, kyōkebi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “くゑ日” (sometimes rendered as “くしえ” or “くしゑ”). It is a day on which the harmony of yin and yang fails, making it a taboo day for all matters; any auspicious undertaking on this day is considered inauspicious. This is one of the older calendrical annotations – in the detailed annotated calendars it is recorded under 24 different names (as indicated in square brackets in the table below). In the Senmei Calendar it appears 82 times per year, and was reduced to 72 times in the Teikyou Calendar. Although various theories exist regarding its allocation, during the Senmei Calendar era it was determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}, whereas from the Teikyou Calendar onward it was determined by the monthly method (based on the {{ill|Old Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}}). Incidentally, in the detailed annotated calendars, on days that are not designated as Kyōkai Days, inscriptions for the Great Age God and the Small Age God – such as “After the Great Age”, “Great/Small Age Position”, or “Before the Great Age, in contrast to the Small Age” – were written; on Kyōkai Days, however, the name corresponding to one of the 24 types of Kyōkai Days was inscribed instead. In kana calendars, the detailed classification of Kyōkai Days was omitted, and only the notation “くゑ日” appears in the lower section.
==== Ōmō Day ==== (Ōmō nichi) literally means “the day to depart and perish.” In ancient times, military campaigns or long journeys were taboo on this day, and official audiences, relocations, or weddings were also considered inauspicious. Ōmō Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} based on the number of days from each month’s seasonal marker. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || 20th day |- | Ox Month || 30th day |- | Tiger Month || 7th day |- | Rabbit Month || 14th day |- | Dragon Month || 21st day |- | Snake Month || 8th day |- | Horse Month || 16th day |- | Goat Month || 24th day |- | Monkey Month || 9th day |- | Rooster Month || 18th day |- | Dog Month || 27th day |- | Pig Month || 10th day |}
==== The Three Bad Days ==== The term “Three Bad Days” (sanga no akunichi) is the collective name for the three inauspicious days: Daimaka Day, Wōryaku Day, and Mettomon Day. Their allocation varies according to the individual’s birth year’s {{ill|Earthly Branches|en|Earthly Branches|WD=Q1072961|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Earthly Branches}}. For example, for someone born in the Year of the Snake, the fourth month (the taboo month) will have its Monkey Day, Rooster Day, and Tiger Day designated as the Three Bad Days; likewise, in January only those born in the Year of the Tiger and in February only those born in the Year of the Rabbit are affected. However, some modern calendars list all the days indicated in the table below as inauspicious for everyone, regardless of one’s birth year. The Three Bad Days should not be used for any auspicious undertaking, and are considered extremely inauspicious for Buddhist ceremonies. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" ! Birth Year !! Taboo Month !! Daimaka Day !! Wōryaku Day !! ===== Daimaka Day ===== (Daimaka nichi) is considered the worst of the Three Bad Days. It is advised to refrain from excessive talk, and to strictly avoid home repairs, construction of doorways, sea voyages, and funerals.
===== Wōryaku Day ===== (Rōshaku nichi) is deemed inauspicious for all undertakings. It is said that engaging in any activity on this day will result in complete failure.
===== Mettomon Day ===== (Metsumon nichi) is regarded as inauspicious in every respect – it is said that acting on this day will, as the name implies, bring ruin to one’s entire family. There is also a day known in the calendrical annotations as “Metsubi” which is considered inauspicious for all matters; however, this arises from a mathematical discrepancy between the ideal 360-day year and the actual year, and is of an entirely different character. Moreover, the term “Metsubi” was abolished during the Teikyou Calendar reform in the Edo period and is no longer reflected in current lunar calendars. (Sometimes, Mettomon Day is abbreviated as “Metsubi,” leading to confusion between the two.)
==== Tokigejiki (Time‐Limited Eating Taboo) ==== (Tokigejiki, also known as Gejikodoki) is a designation for a specific time on a specific day that is considered inauspicious for eating. Like Saigejiki, it refers to the time when the spirit of the '''Tengūsei''' (Tengu Star) – a type of meteor – descends to the earthly realm for the purpose of eating. It is said that if a person eats during this time, all the nutritional value of the food will be absorbed by the spirit, and consuming any leftovers will bring misfortune. In addition to meals, activities such as sowing seeds, opening a rice bag, bathing, and planting are also considered inauspicious during this period. The day and time for Tokigejiki are as follows. The month is determined by the seasonal transition; for example, in January, the Hai period of Goat Day is designated as Tokigejiki. (In calendars from the Teikyou era onward, only the months of May through October are indicated.) Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Ox Day during the Rooster Hour |- | Ox Month || Rabbit Day during the Dog Hour |- | Tiger Month || Goat Day during the Pig Hour |- | Rabbit Month || Dog Day during the Rat Hour |- | Dragon Month || Dragon Day during the Ox Hour |- | Snake Month || Tiger Day during the Tiger Hour |- | Horse Month || Horse Day during the Rabbit Hour |- | Goat Month || Rat Day during the Dragon Hour |- | Monkey Month || Monkey Day during the Snake Hour |- | Rooster Month || Rooster Day during the Horse Hour |- | Dog Month || Snake Day during the Goat Hour |- | Pig Month || Pig Day during the Monkey Hour |}
==== Saigejiki (Year‐Long Eating Taboo) ==== (Saigejiki, also read as Saikajiki) is, like Tokigejiki, the designation for the day on which the spirit of the '''Tengūsei''' (Tengu Star) descends to the earthly realm for the purpose of eating; however, unlike Tokigejiki, Saigejiki is not tied to a specific time. It is considered a mildly inauspicious day, and if another auspicious annotation is present on the same day, there is no need to avoid it; however, if it coincides with other inauspicious days, its effects are compounded. This day is also regarded as a day to refrain from heavy meals and excessive drinking, and, like Tokigejiki, activities such as sowing seeds or opening rice bags and planting are considered inauspicious. Saigejiki is allocated to a specific {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} day that varies according to the individual’s birth year ({{ill|Earthly Branches|en|Earthly Branches|WD=Q1072961|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Earthly Branches}}). The numbers indicate the count from the first Jiazi Day. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Year || 14 || 丁丑日 |- | Ox Year || 27 || 庚寅日 |- | Tiger Year || 4 || 丁卯日 |- | Rabbit Year || 29 || 壬辰日 |- | Dragon Year || 54 || 丁巳日 |- | Snake Year || 43 || 丙午日 |- | Horse Year || 44 || 丁未日 |- | Goat Year || 57 || 庚申日 |- | Monkey Year || 34 || 丁酉日 |- | Rooster Year || 23 || 丙戌日 |- | Dog Year || 48 || 辛亥日 |- | Pig Year || 5 || 庚子日 |}
=== Others ===
==== Juuni Day ==== (Juuni nichi, sometimes written as “Chiu nichi”) is designated on days when the yang (陽) aspect is compounded on Snake Days (巳) and when the yin (陰) is compounded on Pig Days (亥). It is believed that actions performed on this day will have a compounded effect – making auspicious matters even more so and inauspicious matters even worse. However, marriages are considered unfavorable on this day as they may lead to remarriage. Additionally, any day on which the numeral of the month and the day coincide is also referred to as Juuni Day.
==== Fuku Day ==== (Fuku nichi or buku nichi), sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “ぶく日”, is a day on which the effects of any action are said to be doubled – if an auspicious act is undertaken, the auspiciousness is compounded, and if an inauspicious act is undertaken, the misfortune is compounded. However, weddings are considered inauspicious on this day as they may lead to remarriage. Fuku Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month and Horse Month || 丁日 and 癸日 |- | Ox Month, Dragon Month, Goat Month, and Dog Month || 戊日 and 己日 |- | Tiger Month and Monkey Month || 甲日 and 庚日 |- | Rabbit Month and Rooster Month || 乙日 and 辛日 |- | Snake Month and Pig Month || 丙日 and 壬日 |}

'''Rekichū Gedan''' (暦注下段) is the calendrical annotation originally written at the very bottom of the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} that gives the daily auspices (the omens of good and bad fortune). It is also simply called the '''lower section'''. It is based on the divination method of the agricultural calendar – the {{ill|Agricultural Calendar|ja|農暦|lt=Peasant’s Calendar|lt_ja=農民曆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Agricultural Calendar|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中国暦|1=Chinese calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134032}}, which has been handed down since ancient China – and many of its contents (such as Ten‐sha Days and Jushi Days) overlap with those of the peasant’s calendar.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=查詢農民曆─農民曆/農曆/黃曆｜科技紫微網 |url=https://ecal.click108.com.twindex.php/ |website=ecal.click108.com.twindex.php |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=2023農民曆吉時查詢,黃曆通書黃道吉日查詢 - 農民曆查詢 |url=http://www.nongli.info/huangli/ |website=www.nongli.info |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=子易預測網 - 擇日萬年曆 |url=https://forecasting.hk/calendar/ |website=forecasting.hk |access-date=2023-07-20|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=農民曆專有名詞 @ Gloria隨筆 :: 痞客邦 :: |url=http://andafansia.pixnet.net/blog/post/40052541 |website=Gloria隨筆 |date=2011-12-11 |access-date=2023-07-20 |language=zh-TW |last=Andafansia (Andafansia)|qq=}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=你應該懂的農民曆常識！搞懂「當日紀要」神祉，挑對日子趨吉避凶不求人 {{!|qq=}} 食尚玩家 |url=https://supertaste.tvbs.com.tw/hot/321211 |website=TVBS |date=2020-02-06 |access-date=2023-07-20 |last=TVBS|qq=}}</ref>
== List == Originally, in the lower section of the calendrical annotations, the Jushi Day (marked with “●”) and the Jūshi Day (sometimes written as “十し”) were not recorded in duplication with other items, while the other annotations often appeared several times on a single day – and on occasion the lower section was left blank. However, nowadays, with the prominence of systems such as {{ill|Rokuyō|ja|六曜|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rokuyō|qq=}} and {{ill|Nine Stars|ja|九星|1=Nine Stars|2=ja|3=九星|lt=Nine Stars|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nine Stars|qq=}}, the lower section has become rather minor; as a result, contemporary commercially available calendars sometimes omit the lower section entirely, or—if they include it—only record one or two annotations per day, and even if multiple annotations are recorded, even the Jushi or Jūshi Days are often duplicated with others.
In the period from the Meiji era to prewar Shōwa, the lower section of calendrical annotations found in the so‐called {{ill|Obake Calendar|ja|お化け暦|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Obake Calendar|1=Ghost calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11262936}} was not supervised by calendrical experts and frequently did not conform at all to the original method of determining the lower section.
Because the lower section of calendrical annotations is relatively minor in modern Japan, it is seldom included in calendars that use the seven-day format.
=== Auspicious Days === The auspicious days in these lower calendrical annotations are known as the '''Seven Auspicious Days'''.
==== Ten‐sha Day ==== (Tensha nichi, tenshabi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “天しや” and also appears in the {{ill|Day Selection|ja|選日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection|1=Senjitsu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q60988968}}. It is regarded as the day on which the myriad deities ascend to heaven and where heaven forgives the sins of all things – making it the most auspicious day of all. Accordingly, only on Ten‐sha Day is the annotation “万よし” (all is auspicious) added. Ten‐sha Days are determined by the season and the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} and occur five or six times a year. {| class="wikitable" |- | From the start of Spring to the day before the start of Summer || 戊寅日 |- | From the start of Summer to the day before the start of Autumn || 甲午日 |- | From the start of Autumn to the day before the start of Winter || 戊申日 |- | From the start of Winter to the day before the start of Spring || 甲子日 |}
==== Kamiyoshi Day ==== (Kamiyoshi nichi, kamiyoshi bi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “神よし”. It is considered auspicious for matters related to divine rites – that is, for visiting shrines, participating in festivals, and honoring one’s ancestors – while it is inauspicious for impure matters. This calendrical annotation is unique to Japan. Kamiyoshi Days are determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}) and are allocated among the following 33 zodiac designations (the numbers indicate the number of days from the first Jiazi Day, 甲子日):
2乙丑日・4丁卯日・6己巳日・7庚午日・9壬申日・10癸酉日・14丁丑日・16己卯日・19壬午日・21甲申日・22乙酉日・25戊子日・28辛卯日・31甲午日・33丙申日・34丁酉日・36己亥日・37庚子日・38辛丑日・40癸卯日・42乙巳日・43丙午日・44丁未日・45戊申日・46己酉日・48辛亥日・49壬子日・52乙卯日・55戊午日・56己未日・57庚申日・58辛酉日
==== Daimyō Day ==== (Daimyō nichi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “大みやう”. The term “Daimyō” signifies a day when heaven and earth are fully open and the sun shines in every corner, making it extremely auspicious for all benevolent activities. It is especially favorable for construction, relocation, and travel. Daimyō Day first appeared as a calendrical annotation in the Tang dynasty’s {{ill|Daimyō Calendar|ja|大明暦|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daimyō Calendar|1=Q5369150|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5369150}}. It is determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}) and is allocated among the following 25 zodiac designations (the numbers indicate the count from the first Jiazi Day). (There is also a theory that, excluding the four designations 6己巳日, 7庚午日, 44丁未日, and 55戊午日, only 21 types apply.)
6己巳日・7庚午日・8辛未日・9壬申日・10癸酉日・14丁丑日・16己卯日・19壬午日・21甲申日・24丁亥日・29壬辰日・32乙未日・39壬寅日・41甲辰日・42乙巳日・43丙午日・44丁未日・46己酉日・47庚戌日・48辛亥日・53丙辰日・55戊午日・56己未日・57庚申日・58辛酉日
==== Kishuku Day ==== (Kishuku nichi) is determined in the same manner as the auspices of the {{ill|Twenty-Eight Mansions|en|Twenty-Eight Mansions|WD=Q1378760|lt=Twenty‐Eight Mansions|1=Twenty-Eight Mansions}}’ “{{ill|Ghost (Chinese constellation)|en|Ghost (Chinese constellation)|WD=Q1145465|lt=Kishuku|1=Ghost (Chinese constellation)}}.”
==== Tenon Day ==== (Tenon nichi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “天おん”. As its name implies, it is a day on which one receives the blessings of heaven, and is used for auspicious matters – though it must not be used for inauspicious affairs. Tenon Day is determined solely by the day’s {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}} (by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Uninterrupted|lt_ja=不断|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}). Although various theories exist regarding its allocation, the ''Rekirin Mondōshu'' designates the following 15 zodiac days (the numbers indicate the count from the first Jiazi Day):
1甲子日・2乙丑日・3丙寅日・4丁卯日・5戊辰日・16己卯日・17庚辰日・18辛巳日・19壬午日・20癸未日・46己酉日・47庚戌日・48辛亥日・49壬子日・50癸丑日
==== Bosō Day ==== (Bosō nichi) is simply written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as '''母倉'''. It signifies a day when heaven shows benevolence toward humankind in the same way a mother cares for her child, and is one of the '''Seven Auspicious Days'''. Everything is considered auspicious on this day – and marriage in particular is viewed as extremely favorable. Likewise, construction and renovation are also auspicious. Bosō Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated to the following day.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month and Pig Month || Monkey Day and Rooster Day |- | Ox Month, Dragon Month, Goat Month, and Dog Month || Snake Day and Horse Day |- | Tiger Month and Rabbit Month || Rat Day and Pig Day |- | Snake Month and Horse Month || Tiger Day and Rabbit Day |- | Monkey Month and Rooster Month || Ox Day, Dragon Day, Goat Day, and Dog Day |}
==== Tsukitoku Day ==== (Tsukitoku nichi, gattoku nichi) is considered auspicious for activities involving the soil, such as the expansion or renovation of a house. Tsukitoku Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated to the following day.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month, Dragon Month, and Monkey Month || 壬日 |- | Ox Month, Snake Month, and Rooster Month || 庚日 |- | Tiger Month, Horse Month, and Dog Month || 丙日 |- | Rabbit Month, Goat Month, and Pig Month || 甲日 |}
=== Inauspicious Days ===
==== Jushi Day ==== (Jushi nichi, jushibi), also known as the “Black Day” because it is marked with a “●” in the lower section of the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} (and sometimes written simply as “● Day” in modern calendars), is considered the worst of all inauspicious days. It is said that on this day one should not consult any other calendrical annotations, and that if one falls ill on this day, death is inevitable. Illness visits, taking medication, acupuncture, and travel are especially considered unlucky, though holding a funeral is permitted. Jushi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} as follows.
Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Rabbit Day |- | Ox Month || Rooster Day |- | Tiger Month || Dog Day |- | Rabbit Month || Dragon Day |- | Dragon Month || Pig Day |- | Snake Month || Snake Day |- | Horse Month || Rat Day |- | Goat Month || Horse Day |- | Monkey Month || Ox Day |- | Rooster Month || Goat Day |- | Dog Month || Tiger Day |- | Pig Month || Monkey Day |}
==== Jūshi Day ==== (Jūshi nichi) is sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “十し”. It is regarded as inauspicious in every respect – coming immediately after Jushi Day (the Black Day) – and is considered unfavorable for all matters, although unlike Jushi Day, holding a funeral is not strictly prohibited. Jūshi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and follows a repeating cycle of Rooster, Snake, and Ox. ==== Five Tomb Days ==== (Five Tomb Days) vary from person to person according to the nature of the {{ill|Noin|ja|納音|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Noin|1=natchin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10465180}} of one’s birth year, and are determined as shown in the table below. The term “Five Tombs” refers to the fact that the zodiac signs of {{ill|Ox|ja|丑|1=chǒu|lt=Ox (丑)|2=ja|3=丑|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ox|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16539206}}, {{ill|Dragon|ja|辰|1=chén|lt=Dragon (辰)|2=ja|3=辰|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dragon|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16538966}}, {{ill|Goat|ja|未|1=wèi|lt=Goat (未)|2=ja|3=未|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goat|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q20128396}}, and {{ill|Dog (zodiac)|en|Dog (zodiac)|WD=Q755126|lt=Dog (戌)|1=Dog (zodiac)}} – which possess an earth element – designate these five types of zodiac days as Five Tomb Days. All Five Tomb Days are inauspicious; while they pose no problem for building a house, activities such as groundbreaking, foundation laying, funerals, tomb construction, sowing ({{ill|Sowing|en|Sowing|WD=Q777671|lt=Sowing|1=Sowing}}), travel, and prayer are considered unlucky. By its very name, it is said that carrying out such activities (especially funerals) on these days will result in “five tombs” (i.e. the death of five people). {| class="wikitable" |- | (Wood element) || 乙丑日 |- | (Fire element) || 丙戌日 |- | (Earth element) || 戊辰日 |- | (Metal element) || 辛未日 |- | (Water element) || 壬辰日 |}
==== Kiki Day ==== (Kiki nichi, also read as kishibi, kikojitsu, or kiimi nichi) is sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} simply as “きこ”. In modern calendars, even lending or borrowing money is considered inauspicious on this day. ==== Chikibi Day ==== (Chikibi nichi, also read as chii nichi or chikoni nichi) is sometimes written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “ちいみ”. It refers to the influence of the spirit of the ρ, σ, and ε stars of the {{ill|Boötes|en|Boötes|WD=Q8667|lt=Ushikai|1=Boötes}}—which in China are known as “Sakki”, “Nichiki”, and “Chikiki” and are believed to govern a murderous energy. On Chikibi Day, the sight of blood is considered particularly inauspicious, and activities such as acupuncture, capital punishment, and hunting are especially taboo. An ancient calendrical annotation, it is noted in the detailed calendars that “one must not use needles to draw blood on this day.” Chikibi Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows.

==== Tenka Day ==== (Tenka nichi, tenka bi), corresponding to {{ill|Chika Day|ja|地火日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chika Day|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 暦注下段|1=Rekichū Gedan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11514957}}, is also known as one of the “Five Poor Days.” According to the Five Elements theory, fire is divided into three types—heavenly fire, earthly fire, and human fire—with Tenka referring to the severe fire of heaven. It is said that if one undertakes activities such as raising a roof or re-roofing on a Tenka Day, a fire is inevitable. Likewise, repairs to a house or relocation (in the sense of a distinguished person moving) are considered inauspicious. Tenka Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows. (Its allocation is exactly the same as that for Wōryaku Day, one of the Three Bad Days.) ==== Chika Day (“Shishin” in the Agricultural Calendar) ==== (Chika nichi, chika bi) corresponds to Tenka Day. In the Chinese {{ill|Agricultural Calendar|ja|農暦|lt=Peasant’s Calendar|lt_ja=農民曆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Agricultural Calendar|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中国暦|1=Chinese calendar|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q134032}}, it is called “'''Shishin'''” (the God of Death) and is treated as equivalent to Jushi Day. According to the Five Elements theory, fire is divided into heavenly, earthly, and human fire, with “earthly fire” referring to the severe fire of the earth. On Chika Day, activities such as groundbreaking, laying foundations, erecting pillars, well digging, sowing ({{ill|Sowing|en|Sowing|WD=Q777671|lt=Sowing|1=Sowing}}), tomb construction, and funerals are considered inauspicious. Chika Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} and is allocated as follows. This allocation is exactly the same as that for “Hira” in the Twelve Directives, although what is deemed inauspicious on Chika Day is considered auspicious under “Hira,” resulting in a contradiction. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" |- | Rat Month || Rabbit Day |- | Ox Month || Dragon Day |- | Tiger Month || Snake Day |- | Rabbit Month || Horse Day |- | Dragon Month || Goat Day |- | Snake Month || Monkey Day |- | Horse Month || Rooster Day |- | Goat Month || Dog Day |- | Monkey Month || Pig Day |- | Rooster Month || Rat Day |- | Dog Month || Ox Day |- | Pig Month || Tiger Day |}
==== Kyōkai Day ==== (Kyōkai nichi, kyōkebi) is written in the {{ill|Calendar|en|Calendar|WD=Q12132|lt=Calendar|1=Calendar}} as “くゑ日” (sometimes rendered as “くしえ” or “くしゑ”). It is a day on which the harmony of yin and yang fails, making it a taboo day for all matters; any auspicious undertaking on this day is considered inauspicious. This is one of the older calendrical annotations – in the detailed annotated calendars it is recorded under 24 different names (as indicated in square brackets in the table below). In the Senmei Calendar it appears 82 times per year, and was reduced to 72 times in the Teikyou Calendar. Although various theories exist regarding its allocation, during the Senmei Calendar era it was determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}}, whereas from the Teikyou Calendar onward it was determined by the monthly method (based on the {{ill|Old Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}}). Kyōkai Day is fixed for each month by assigning a specific {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Sexagenary cycle}}; in the table below the items in parentheses were abolished in the Teikyou Calendar (with <sup>●</sup> indicating those overlapping with Jushi Day and <sup>十</sup> those overlapping with Jūshi Day). Incidentally, in the detailed annotated calendars, on days that are not designated as Kyōkai Days, inscriptions for the Great Age God and the Small Age God – such as “After the Great Age”, “Great/Small Age Position”, or “Before the Great Age, in contrast to the Small Age” – were written; on Kyōkai Days, however, the name corresponding to one of the 24 types of Kyōkai Days was inscribed instead. In kana calendars, the detailed classification of Kyōkai Days was omitted, and only the notation “くゑ日” appears in the lower section.
==== Ōmō Day ==== (Ōmō nichi) literally means “the day to depart and perish.” In ancient times, military campaigns or long journeys were taboo on this day, and official audiences, relocations, or weddings were also considered inauspicious. Ōmō Day is determined by the {{ill|Day Selection Method|ja|撰日法|lt=Seasonal Transition|lt_ja=節切り|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Day Selection Method|1=Senpō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11498765}} based on the number of days from each month’s seasonal marker. ==== The Three Bad Days ==== The term “Three Bad Days” (sanga no akunichi) is the collective name for the three inauspicious days: Daimaka Day, Wōryaku Day, and Mettomon Day. Their allocation varies according to the individual’s birth year’s {{ill|Earthly Branches|en|Earthly Branches|WD=Q1072961|lt=Chinese Zodiac|1=Earthly Branches}}. For example, for someone born in the Year of the Snake, the fourth month (the taboo month) will have its Monkey Day, Rooster Day, and Tiger Day designated as the Three Bad Days; likewise, in January only those born in the Year of the Tiger and in February only those born in the Year of the Rabbit are affected. However, some modern calendars list all the days indicated in the table below as inauspicious for everyone, regardless of one’s birth year. The Three Bad Days should not be used for any auspicious undertaking, and are considered extremely inauspicious for Buddhist ceremonies. Note: The month is determined by the seasonal transition. {| class="wikitable" ! Birth Year !! Taboo Month !! Daimaka Day !! Wōryaku Day !!
